March and March

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a country still wrestling with inequality and high unemployment, a grassroots movement led by a former radio personality is demanding action on illegal immigration — and dividing public opinion

Unique Selling Point:
March and March: Until We Win” takes viewers into the streets, homes, and halls of power in South Africa to unpack what this controversial campaign says about race, justice, and who truly belongs.


Summary:
Launched in March 2025 by Jacinta Zinhle MaNgobese Zuma, a former broadcaster turned activist, the “March and March” campaign calls for action against illegal immigration in South Africa. The movement insists it is not xenophobic, but patriotic — fighting for local jobs, strained public services, and what it sees as the erosion of citizen rights.
The story follows the campaign from its inception in KwaZulu-Natal to its growing national momentum. Through emotional testimonies, tense protests, and intimate moments with organisers and critics alike, March and Marchinvestigates the real grievances behind the placards — and whether these marches signal empowerment, desperation, or dangerous scapegoating.

Press Release:


March and March
In a country wrestling with historic inequality and growing unemployment, a grassroots movement is demanding action on illegal immigration — and dividing public opinion. Led by a former radio personality, the “March and March” campaign insists it is not xenophobic, but patriotic: fighting for local jobs and against the strain on public services and what it sees as the erosion of citizen rights. We follow the controversial campaign from its inception in KwaZulu-Natal to its growing national momentum, and unpack what it says about race, justice, and who truly belongs.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


SCRIPT | MARCH AND MARCH


(Facebook Video Subtitle) We don’t allow foreigners here. ID. Identify yourself.

(Upsound Newscast) Foreign nationals in South Africa are once again at the center of debate over public health care services.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Chris Hani Baragwanath doesn't allow foreigners anymore.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) But I showed you my permit just now.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Wait, wait -ID.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Who are you? Who are you?

(Facebook Video Subtitle) You’re not the police, boy.

(Upsound Newscast) A group called March and March has blocked off the entrance to local clinics once again.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) You’re not immigration. This is my ID. This gives me the right.
You don’t have a right!

(Upsound Newscast) They argue that the healthcare facilities are mostly overwhelmed by illegal immigrants who compromise the standard of care for citizens.

(Macfarlane) Earlier this year, a group calling itself March and March began blocking foreigners from accessing public hospitals.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) We’re tired of illegal immigrants in South Africa. They’re the reason for most of our problems.

(Macfarlane) March and March claims it’s defending scarce resources, but its critics argue what it’s doing is illegal, a violation of human rights and our laws.01:14 - 01:19

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Overcrowded hospitals?

(Facebook Video Subtitle) They’re responsible!

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Dirty Buildings?

(Facebook Video Subtitle) They’re responsible!

(Macfarlane) In a country where public healthcare is failing, who gets to decide WHO receives care — and who doesn’t?

(Facebook Video Subtitle) We’re tired of illegal immigrants in South Africa. They’re the reason for most of our problems.

(Macfarlane) March and March claims it’s defending scarce resources, but its critics argue what it’s doing is illegal, a violation of human rights and our laws.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Overcrowded hospitals?

(Facebook Video Subtitle) They’re responsible!

(Facebook Video Subtitle) Dirty Buildings?

(Facebook Video Subtitle) They’re responsible!

((Macfarlane) ) In a country where public healthcare is failing, who gets to decide WHO receives care — and who doesn’t?

(Macfarlane) Our public healthcare system is buckling from years of under-resourcing, neglect and mismanagement. There’s only one doctor for every 3,000 patients.

(Macfarlane) Like most other provinces, hospitals in KwaZulu-Natal are understaffed, equipment is failing and there’s not enough medicine to go around.


(Facebook Video Subtitle) Every time I come there's a shortage of medication and I am a South African citizen.

(Macfarlane) According to March and March founder, Jacinta Zuma, illegal immigration is robbing South Africans of healthcare. That, she says, is why they’re taking a hard line against undocumented migrants.

(Jacinta) Go and get there and find that there's no medication, and you're sick and you're desperate

(Macfarlane) Zuma works in media and has a sizeable social media following.



(Macfarlane) After venting online about undocumented foreign nationals, she noted many of the responses focused on their impact on healthcare.

(Jacinta) I had an idea that, okay, we're going to march. And maybe marching in March is actually a good idea. We've marched, but obviously that doesn't mean that the problem is solved.

(Macfarlane) After that initial march, Zuma decided to continue her campaign.

(Jacinta) And then I thought, okay, maybe let's change the name March in March to March and March, which is basically a concept that says that until our voices are heard, we don't stop.

(Macfarlane) Despite it being illegal to turn away anyone needing emergency healthcare from public hospitals, Zuma and her movement are blocking access to all except South African citizens and permanent residents.

(Jacinta) We go to hospitals and clinics and we make sure that we verify people's documentation.

(Macfarlane) That means stopping everyone at hospital entrances and demanding that they recite their South African ID numbers.


(Upsound Citizen) 063233.

(Macfarlane) If that fails, they’re asked for their clan name or, in the case of foreigners, to prove their permanent residency. Asylum documents aren’t accepted. It’s a puzzling sight: locals generally co-operating, foreigners nervously queuing, while people openly break the law. Not a police officer to be seen.

(Macfarlane) This entrance has become a flashpoint. Members of the March and March campaign have been blocking foreign nationals from entering saying that public healthcare services are over stretched and overwhelmed.

(Macfarlane) It’s a context impossible to dispute, and a situation many familiar with the decline in public health have been warning about for years.

(Macfarlane) Pretty Miya has weekly cancer treatment at Durban’s Addington Hospital. She’s also a member of March and March.


(Pretty) You would have to arrive at 4 AM.

(Macfarlane) 4 am?

(Pretty) Yes, the latest five o’clock.

(Pretty) Then you get in and wait until 7 o'clock

(Pretty) when they open for the admin to start capturing people.

02:16 - When you arrive at the doctors, you sit until 4 pm.

(Macfarlane) That’s a 12 hour wait…for someone battling cancer.

(Macfarlane) Nhlanhla Mqadi considers himself a patriot.

(Nhlanhla) We're exhausted, we're stressed, we're overpopulated. We are not taken serious as citizens.

(Macfarlane) Today, Nhlanhla stopped this woman from entering the hospital. She's from Malawi and wasn’t allowed to see her grandchild who’s receiving treatment.

(Malawian Woman Subtitle) I cant see my granddaughter.

(Malawian Woman Subtitle) If you never got ID you can’t go inside.

(Malawian Woman Subtitle) I can't do anything.

(Macfarlane) The significant problems in public health aside, stories like this underscore the cruelty in March and March’s methods. And it’s not limited to foreigners.

(Macfarlane) This video shows an elderly South African being man handled for refusing to show his ID to strangers.

(Macfarlane) He’s being assaulted by Pretty Miya, the cancer patient we interviewed earlier.

(Percy) When you get somebody coming to a health facility either injured or very sick. The last thing you are going to do is to say, Where is your identity document? Where do you come from?

(Macfarlane) Dr. Percy Mahlati is Deputy Director-General of Hospitals at the Department of Health.

(Macfarlane) He says only certain agencies like the police or Home Affairs officials are allowed to ask for ID to check citizenship.

(Percy) If I'm a doctor in a clinic or a hospital and somebody is brought I'm actually required,to save that life, because if I were to withhold on the basis that this is somebody who's a foreigner, I don't have the ability to determine whether it's legal or illegal, 8:12 and if that soul passes away, I actually have to answer.

(Mcfarlane) What the March and March volunteers are doing is illegal.

(Marfarlane) You're not a police, you're not home affairs, you're not an official. What authority do you have to stop people from getting public services?

(Nhlanhla) Law enforcement inside the city, inside the country, is not doing it. Must I sit and watch my country collapse?

(Macfarlane) Don't you think what you're doing is problematic, for South Africans who might feel insulted that they are being asked to produce their IDs irrespective of being citizens of this country?

(Pretty) 06:16 - No, I don't see it as a problem. I think it's beneficial to them.

(Macfarlane) The insult suffered by locals pales against the more serious consequences for people denied health care, but neither sits comfortably.

(Macfarlane) we fought so hard for the right to eliminate the dom pass. And being a South African and asked to identify myself in my own country is not easy to swallow.

(Pretty) On many occasions, you come here and find that there are no beds in the wards. Even if you’re too sick, they say the wards are full, full of foreign nationals.
(Macfarlane) It’s a widely held view – not just in KZN – but verifying the claim is impossible. It’s not known how many foreigners are in South Africa illegally, never mind how many rely on public healthcare.

(Kgosi) It's not immigration policies, it's policing. There are certain policies of the government that have put us where we are, making us a borderless country. Is turning us into being no country at all.

(Macfarlane) ActionSA’s Dr Kgosi Letlape, says the root of the problem lies with immigration laws that aren’t enforced.

(Kgosi) After you have received care, if you are undocumented, you are handed over to the relevant authorities to sort out your status in this country. When you have that failure, you're going to end up with vigilantism.

(Macfarlane) It’s a perfect storm: porous borders, under-resourcing and crumbling infrastructure fueling growing resentment, even among people like Zuma, who don’t use the system themselves.

(Macfarlane) As March and March continues to barricade hospitals, officials have been mostly silent or looked the other way.

(Macfarlane) Without clear action from authorities, tensions are rising.

(Facebook Video Subtitle) We are at Addington, they are refusing security to close the gate and pushing it away.

(Subtitle) You will never get help here, mama. You? You will never.

(Macfarlane) The Constitution says everyone has a right to healthcare and that, according to Letlape, is the problem.

(Kgosi) Everyone is not doable. Everyone is a recipe for disaster. What does everyone mean? Does it mean the 60 odd million South Africans, or the 1.1 billion in the continent, or the 8 billion in the globe?We're not saviors of the world. We are just ordinary citizens.
What gripped us was a vicious government policy of apartheid, and all of us need to recover, and the first priority is to ensure that we save our citizens

(Jacinta) I feel like before you just say xenophobia, xenophobia. Have they addressed the concerns of the people?

(Macfarlane) With apparently little appetite by the state to enforce the law, there’s a danger legitimate grievances over the collapse of state services could spiral out of control.

(Jacinta) Ok, but why are you fighting? Why fight when there is no one fighting with you? I just feel like it's a fight and I'm prepared to go fight every day.


(Facebook Video Upsound) We still have a long way to go since our first march. We will march again and again. Is anyone here tired already?”

(Macfarlane) Despite Zuma’s protestations ours is a country all too familiar with how quickly protest can turn into violent xenophobia?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In a country still wrestling with inequality and high unemployment, a grassroots movement led by a former radio personality is demanding action on illegal immigration — and dividing public opinion
metadata.Unique Selling Point: March and March: Until We Win” takes viewers into the streets, homes, and halls of power in South Africa to unpack what this controversial campaign says about race, justice, and who truly belongs.
metadata.Summary: Launched in March 2025 by Jacinta Zinhle MaNgobese Zuma, a former broadcaster turned activist, the “March and March” campaign calls for action against illegal immigration in South Africa. The movement insists it is not xenophobic, but patriotic — fighting for local jobs, strained public services, and what it sees as the erosion of citizen rights. The story follows the campaign from its inception in KwaZulu-Natal to its growing national momentum. Through emotional testimonies, tense protests, and intimate moments with organisers and critics alike, March and Marchinvestigates the real grievances behind the placards — and whether these marches signal empowerment, desperation, or dangerous scapegoating.
